note: A woman brought witnesses to court for her case, and they were shown to be liars. She brought more witnesses, and they too were shown to be liars. She brought a third set, who were not. Reish Lakish said she now had a presumption of dishonesty. Rabbi Elazar answered: if she does, does all of Israel? On another occasion, Reish Lakish and Rabbi Elazar were sitting before Rabbi Yohanan when a similar case came up. Reish Lakish said the same thing, and Rabbi Yohanan answered exactly as Rabbi Elazar had. Reish Lakish turned and glared at Rabbi Elazar: you heard this from bar Nappaha and did not tell me in his name?
why: The mishna has a dispute: if one set of witnesses proves several others to be false, Rabbi Yehuda calls it a conspiracy. The Gemara then asks whether Reish Lakish and Rabbi Yohanan follow Rabbi Yehuda and the Rabbis.

people.name: Reish Lakish
people.about: A Sage who held that the woman's witnesses could no longer be trusted.

people.name: Rabbi Elazar
people.about: A Sage who disagreed with Reish Lakish, as Rabbi Yohanan later did, without saying whose view it was.

people.name: Rabbi Yohanan
people.about: The teacher before whom the second case came; also called bar Nappaha.

people.name: a certain woman
people.about: A litigant whose first two sets of witnesses were proven liars.

terms.meaning: A standing assumption a court makes about someone from their past behavior; here, that she is dishonest.
'Son of the smith', another name for Rabbi Yohanan.

note: Rabbi Yehuda ben Tabbai swore that he had once, as a judge, had a single conspiring witness put to death, to root out the Sadducees' view that such witnesses are killed only after the accused has been executed. Shimon ben Shatah told him he had shed innocent blood, since the Sages taught that conspiring witnesses are executed or flogged only if both are proven conspiring. At once Rabbi Yehuda ben Tabbai resolved never to rule except in the presence of Shimon ben Shatah. All his life he threw himself down on that witness's grave, and his voice was heard. People thought it was the dead man's voice. He told them it was his own, and they would know: when he died, it would no longer be heard.
why: The mishna that follows teaches that a group of false witnesses is punished only when all of them are proven conspiring, which is the rule Shimon ben Shatah holds against him.

people.name: Rabbi Yehuda ben Tabbai
people.about: A judge who had one conspiring witness executed and mourned at his grave for the rest of his life.

people.name: Shimon ben Shatah
people.about: His colleague, who told him he had shed innocent blood.

people.name: the Sadducees
people.about: A Jewish group who disagreed with the Sages about when conspiring witnesses are executed.

terms.meaning: A witness proven false by others who testify he was elsewhere at the time. The Torah gives him the punishment he tried to bring on the accused.

terms.term: I will not see the consolation
terms.meaning: A form of oath: may I not see the future comfort of the Jewish people if what I say is untrue.

note: Rav Hisda was sitting and studying in the study hall of Rav, and the agent of the Angel of Death could not come near him, because his mouth never stopped studying. The agent went up and sat on the cedar tree of the study hall. The cedar broke, Rav Hisda fell silent for a moment, and the agent overcame him.
why: Rabbi Yohanan said that words of Torah give refuge. The Gemara offers that this means refuge from the Angel of Death, and the story shows the protection holds only while one is actually studying.

people.name: Rav Hisda
people.about: A Sage whose constant study kept the Angel of Death away until a noise made him stop.

people.name: the agent of the Angel of Death
people.about: Sent to take Rav Hisda's life; he breaks the cedar to interrupt him.

terms.meaning: The angel sent to take a person's life when their time comes.
Protect, as the cities of refuge protected someone who killed by accident. Here it means protection from death.

note: A teacher of children was negligent in watching over them, and Rav Aha made a vow that he would no longer teach. Ravina restored him to his post anyway, because no other teacher could be found who was as accurate as he was.
why: The Gemara has just ruled that a vow made with the public's consent can be undone when undoing it serves a mitzva. This case is brought as proof: teaching children is a mitzva, so the teacher's ban was lifted.

people.name: Rav Aha
people.about: A Sage who vowed that the negligent teacher would no longer teach.

people.name: Ravina
people.about: A Sage who restored the teacher because no one else was as accurate.

terms.term: vow on the consent of the public
terms.meaning: A vow made with the community's agreement, normally treated as impossible to undo. The translation reads Rav Aha's vow this way.

note: Rav Yehuda ruled that anyone who eats a fish-like creature found in the furrows left by a plow is flogged, for breaking the ban on eating creeping things. A man once ate such a creature, and Rav Yehuda had him flogged.
why: The mishna lists who receives lashes, including one who eats creeping animals. The Gemara now goes through specific creatures, and here Rav Yehuda carries out his own ruling.

people.name: Rav Yehuda
people.about: A Sage who ruled that eating this creature earns lashes, and then had a man flogged for it.

terms.meaning: Given lashes, the court's punishment for breaking certain Torah prohibitions.
Small crawling creatures such as insects and reptiles, which the Torah forbids as food.
Animals with a fatal injury or defect, forbidden as food even if properly slaughtered.

flag: The STORY is mostly a legal ruling; the incident itself is one sentence, a man who ate the creature and was flogged.

note: Rabban Gamliel, Rabbi Elazar ben Azarya, Rabbi Yehoshua and Rabbi Akiva were walking on the road when they heard the noise of the crowds of Rome from Puteoli, a hundred and twenty mil away. The others began to weep, and Rabbi Akiva laughed. They asked why he laughed; he asked why they wept. They said: these gentiles, who bow to idols, live secure and at peace, while our Temple has been burned by fire; shall we not weep? Akiva answered: that is why I laugh. If those who go against God's will are given this much, those who do His will shall be given all the more.
why: The Gemara has been discussing Rav's fear of the curse 'you shall be lost among the nations' and the answers that soften it. The story belongs to that theme of exile and the hope of redemption.

people.name: Rabbi Akiva
people.about: Laughs while his companions weep, and explains why.

people.name: Rabban Gamliel
people.about: One of the four Sages walking on the road.

people.name: Rabbi Elazar ben Azarya
people.about: One of the four Sages walking on the road.

people.name: Rabbi Yehoshua
people.about: One of the four Sages walking on the road.

terms.meaning: A unit of distance, roughly a kilometer.

terms.term: the House of the footstool of our God
terms.meaning: A name for the Temple in Jerusalem, which had been destroyed.

note: On another occasion the same Sages were going up to Jerusalem. At Mount Scopus they tore their clothes, and at the Temple Mount they saw a fox come out of the place of the Holy of Holies. They wept; Rabbi Akiva laughed. They said: the place where an outsider who comes near shall die, now foxes walk in it, and shall we not weep? Akiva said that was why he laughed. Isaiah names Uriah, of the First Temple period, and Zechariah, of the Second, together as witnesses; the verse makes Zechariah's prophecy depend on Uriah's. The text does not give the rest of Akiva's explanation or how the others responded.
why: The Gemara has just told how Akiva laughed at the sound of Rome while the others wept. This is a second time the same Sages weep and Akiva laughs, again over the ruin of the Temple.

people.name: Rabbi Akiva
people.about: Laughs at the sight of the fox and explains it from the prophets.

people.name: Uriah the priest
people.about: A prophet of the First Temple period named in the verse Akiva quotes.

people.name: Zechariah the son of Jeberechiah
people.about: A prophet of the Second Temple period named in the same verse.

terms.meaning: The innermost room of the Temple, where only the High Priest entered, once a year.
A hill outside Jerusalem from which the Temple site could be seen; the Sages tore their clothes there in mourning.

terms.term: the non-priest who approaches shall die
terms.meaning: A Torah verse warning that anyone not a priest who comes near the holy place will die.

flag: The STORY stops in the middle of Akiva's answer: the two prophecies themselves and the Sages' reply, 'Akiva, you have comforted us', are in the AFTER segment.
